rationale: B wins because it trims the set to three real shapes and refuses the padded trend thesis A keeps. Its "Rivian's next revenue line is selling electricity to everyone else's EVs" gives a markets reporter a clean P&L question; A's "following the industry's shift away from automaker-exclusive plugs" leans on an industry narrative the supplied facts don't establish. A has usable bones, but B is the set a founder can brief against without first scraping off the varnish.
gaps_in_A: "following the industry's shift away from automaker-exclusive plugs" is not in the supplied update; it may be true, but this set treats outside context as a foundation before proving it.
"Rivian fields a rival to Tesla's Supercharger network" overstates Rivian's competitive posture. The facts give NACS plugs and open access, not a Tesla-challenge strategy.
The first and fourth angles are too close: "brand-agnostic fast-charging grid" and "rival to Tesla's Supercharger network" are both infrastructure-market-structure stories wearing different jackets.
"newest brand-agnostic fast-charging grid" needs ranking/context proof before it can carry a headline; the update only gives 3,500+ chargers, not market position.
gaps_in_B: "whether opening the network dilutes a perk existing owners bought into" is a sharp question, but it needs proof Rivian actually sold exclusivity as a perk before anyone pitches owner backlash.
"announced today" is slightly too confident from the provided facts. The update says access is live now; it does not explicitly say the announcement date.

The next step starts with "journalist-fit-check" before naming how to build the candidate pool. It should first pick the angle, get the missing price/rollout numbers, then find and fit-check reporters.
